author: potuz
content: No, my main concern is P2P propagation itself. By allowing to broadcast a bid that is not compatible with my view of the chain I'm allowing for arbitrary objects to propagate that are useless. If the parent block has 100% of the vote and I send a bid on top of grandparent with a ridiculously high value I'm guaranteed to reach every node in the chain. I can do this at no cost since my bid is unincludable. I believe this is a bad design for the P2P stack.  It's akin to sending a block based on 32 slots ago, just that I don't lose anything and I can do it every slot

author: jtraglia
content:
According to claude it won't work because of [this condition](https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/blob/e656e15e19cd68f0ca8b87dbf086bc33de90af9c/specs/gloas/fork-choice.md?plain=1#L426-L427).

> Calling should_build_on_full directly doesn't do what it looks like: it branches on get_current_slot, so for a next-slot bid (which gossip allows) it short-circuits to plain head.payload_status and never reaches the timeliness and DA checks. For every bid arriving before the proposal slot it's therefore identical to the strict version, and it diverges precisely in the case we care about — the PTC rules the payload late, the proposer switches to empty, but those bids were already dropped. Passing bid.slot instead doesn't help, since PTC votes are still landing mid-slot and payload_timeliness counts them against a threshold, so accept/reject would flip within a single slot. It also ties propagation to local PTC tallies, so a bid can fail to reach the proposer if a peer on the path disagrees.  Instead, when the head is FULL we accept both the full and the empty parent hash — since should_build_on_full can only ever be more pessimistic than fork choice (an EMPTY head always yields empty), that's a provable superset of every choice a proposer can make, it depends on no local state, and it costs one extra bid per builder per slot.
